chapter: Handedness and Gene Austin in California
title: Leaving his nightclub to join Austin and the union fine
summary: He sells his interest in a club for Austin's offer, then finds Austin's group is non-union and the union fines him.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Oh, I know where we were. We were talking about the men in the band. You were going to tell us. Yeah. You took Candy's place.

Yeah, well, I took Candy went with, I took your cigarette. Yeah, Candy Candido, he quit to go with Ted Fiorita. And that's when Gene sent for me. And at the time, I was part owner of a nightclub. Out here, originally it was the Honeysuckle, and then it got to be the Golden Pumpkin. And the place in there, it was a summer place. It drew good in the summer. Winter wasn't no good at all because right under the lake it used to get a lot of fog out there. People wouldn't come out in the winter clubs. And they had to run what you call a two-bits club. Everything was two-bits. Coke was two-bits. Sandwich, two-bits. Ice, two-bits, you know. And you had to bring your own bottle. So after the summer season was over, the old Italian fellow that owned the place, says to the fellas in the band, says, I'll give you the place. I said, you run at the place. I said, I'll give it to you. She said, you're taking my son. She had a son. So he, and I think it was Jack Otto, I don't know whether you ever met Jack. He used to be a drummer around here. Charlie DuPont and myself had the business. So wound up, at the end of the week, after we paid the band off, and you couldn't cheat, none of them, they wouldn't make a penny on the scale or anything, you know, because I had the Danton sisters playing with, the two Danton boys, you know, had them playing in the band. I think I used to make around $8, $10, maybe $12 a week for myself out of it. So I get this, I get this wire from Austin, see, so I called him. So I told him, I said, what does it pay? He said, well, this, right now, the job we're working right now pays $100 and a quarter. So I said, well, you'll have to send me some car fare. He said, it's all right. So he sent me $150, you see. And, so I sold my interest in the club, for, we used to call them oyster whites, they were white linen suit, they used to wear around here a lot. Some of them, some of the guys still wear them. Oyster white linen, I sold for, for oyster white and a pair of slacks. And, I get out there, I find out, Bill, that the, it's non-union. You see, Austin had to, he had had a review, and it broke up, that, that, that, that, that Lewis lost money, and it broke up, and he, that he owed the, the union $1,100, you see. Well, as long as we worked in it, so, after I got out there, he told us, we ain't union, you know. So I said, what the hell I'm gonna do now? Well, there wasn't no, no figuring on coming back home, because I was stuck, I was out there then, and I owed him the $150 that he sent me. So, long as we worked at this L-Rater, it didn't bother us, but when we got the job at the Grove, well, then the union grabbed us, you see. So they had us all up there before the board. So, Austin had to pay the, the $1,100, and they fined him $1,000. So they got Coco in there, and they asked Coco, did you ever belong to the union? No, sir. I said, well, no, didn't you belong to the Mobile, local, so-and-so? Yes, sir. Didn't you belong to Miami, local? Yes, sir. So they had the bass player the same way. He was a kid from Texas, and he was working around for him, and I sent for him, and got him out there, after I got out there. So, asked him the same thing. Did you belong to such-and-such union in Texas? No, sir. And they had it right there, black and white. They knew they were lying, you see. So, they sent him out, and they called me in there. He said, you ever belong to the union? I said, yes, sir. I said, what union? I said, local 174. He said, why'd you quit? I said, I didn't quit. He said, what you mean, you in the union now? I said, yeah. But I said, here's my card. Paid up in New Orleans, you see. I said, what you doing working out there with this non-union outfit? So, I told him, I said, mister, if a man made you come 2,000 miles away from home, and you come out there and find out it was non-union, what would you do? So, I said, how much a week are you making? So, I told him, I said, well, we make 100 in the car, and that's the salary. I said, but we make $100 a week tips. And they thought I was crazy, because the scale out there, I think, in those days, this is 1934, I think the scale was...
